title: India's IT Giants Are Heading Into a 'Perfect Storm.' Their 200,000 Workers in America Feel It First.
excerpt: AI is eating the $315 billion industry's traditional business model. TCS reports Thursday, and nine brokerages are bracing for another grim quarter.
body:
India's $315 billion IT services industry is heading into what nine major brokerages are calling a "perfect storm" — and the hundreds of thousands of Indian tech workers in the United States are watching their employers' fortunes dim in real time.

Tata Consultancy Services reports its April-June quarter earnings on Thursday, followed by Infosys, HCLTech, and Wipro later this month. The numbers, analysts say, will not be pretty. Strip out the flattering effect of the rupee's sharp depreciation against the dollar, and India's top six IT firms are expected to post a mere 2.8 percent revenue growth in constant-currency terms — in a quarter that is traditionally their strongest.

The Nifty IT index has plunged 28 percent so far in 2026, making information technology the worst-performing major sector on India's stock exchanges. In the June quarter alone, the IT index fell 9.5 percent even as the benchmark Nifty 50 gained 6.9 percent.

## The AI Squeeze

The culprit is not a recession. It is artificial intelligence.

Companies across the globe are rapidly deploying AI tools and agents to cut costs and accelerate software development cycles — precisely the kind of labor-intensive work that built India's IT empire over three decades. Clients are not cutting IT budgets so much as redirecting them: vendor consolidation, cost-optimization projects, and AI-led efficiency gains are replacing the headcount-heavy engagements that fueled Infosys and TCS's growth.



> **""Indian IT firms are in a perfect storm," Nomura said in its earnings preview, citing AI-driven pricing pressure compounded by Middle East conflict-led geopolitical uncertainty."**


"Indian IT firms are in a perfect storm," Nomura said in its earnings preview, citing AI-driven pricing pressure compounded by Middle East conflict-led geopolitical uncertainty.

Citi expects a fourth straight year of subdued growth. JPMorgan sees revenue growth staying below 3 to 4 percent for the "foreseeable future."

TCS Chairman N. Chandrasekaran has said the "day is not far" when the company would have an equal number of AI agents and employees. Last July, TCS cut more than 12,000 jobs; headcount fell by over 23,000 on a net basis in the fiscal year ended March 2026.

## A Diverging Labor Market

The shift is creating a stark divergence in India's tech job market. AI hiring surged 16 percent year-on-year in June, even as overall IT recruitment declined 3 percent, according to job portal Naukri's monthly JobSpeak report.

"The divergence is important because it shows where tech companies are still investing," said Hitesh Oberoi, CEO of Info Edge, which owns Naukri. "AI is increasingly becoming a core capability area, especially as demand shifts towards more senior and specialised talent."

Companies are also buying what they cannot build fast enough. Persistent Systems acquired German firm Nagarro for $1.4 billion. Coforge bought Encora for $2.35 billion. TCS, Infosys, Wipro, and Cognizant have all announced acquisitions aimed at bolting on AI capabilities.

## The Diaspora Impact

For the estimated 200,000-plus Indian IT professionals working in the United States on H-1B visas — many of them employed by or contracted through TCS, Infosys, Wipro, and Cognizant — the earnings season carries personal stakes.

These companies remain among the largest H-1B sponsors in America. A structural downturn in their core business model does not just affect stock prices in Mumbai; it affects hiring pipelines, project assignments, and visa sponsorship decisions in New Jersey, Texas, and California.

The $100,000 H-1B fee — recently struck down by a federal judge but facing an appeal from the Trump administration — had already forced these firms to rethink their U.S. staffing strategies. Combined with AI-led deflation in billable work, the math is getting harder.

For Indian professionals on the ground, the message is increasingly clear: the traditional IT services career path — join a major Indian firm, get posted to the U.S. on an H-1B, and work your way toward a green card — is being rewritten by forces on both sides of the Pacific.

*Sources: Reuters, The Hindu BusinessLine, Livemint, Outlook Business*
